beats.intro: Chapter three. [[sub]]How big is an economy, what moves it up and down, and what makes it grow.
beats.gdp: [[a]]Gross domestic product is the market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a period. [[w]]Take bread. The farmer sells wheat for one hundred. [[m]]The miller turns it into flour and sells it for one hundred forty. [[b]]The baker sells bread for two hundred. [[va]]Count each stage's value added: one hundred, forty, and sixty. [[sum]]They add up to two hundred, the price of the final loaf. Count only final goods, or you count the same wheat three times.
beats.approaches: [[a]]Output has a mirror. Every euro of output is also someone's income, and someone's spending. [[o]]So GDP can be measured by output, [[e]]by expenditure, [[i]]or by income. All three give the same number.
beats.expend: [[a]]The expenditure approach adds up what is bought. [[c]]Consumption, by households. [[i]]Investment, by firms: machines, buildings, and inventories. [[g]]Government spending on goods and services. [[nx]]And net exports: exports, minus imports. [[tot]]Together they make GDP.
beats.realnom: [[a]]Nominal GDP uses current prices, so it can rise just because prices rise. [[n]]Say nominal GDP grows from one hundred to one hundred ten. [[d]]But prices rose seven percent: the GDP deflator is one oh seven. [[r]]Real GDP is nominal GDP divided by the deflator, times one hundred. That is about one hundred two point eight. [[g]]So real growth is about two point eight percent, not ten.
beats.saving: [[a]]Saving, investment, the budget and trade are linked. [[s]]Private saving, on the left, [[i]]pays for investment by firms, [[f]]for the government's deficit, spending minus taxes, [[t]]and for net exports, which is lending to the rest of the world. [[eq]]Saving equals investment, plus the fiscal deficit, plus the trade surplus. The two sides always match.
beats.ad: [[a]]Aggregate demand is total planned spending on domestic output, at each price level. [[curve]]It slopes down: a higher price level means less real GDP demanded. [[w]]Higher prices shrink the real value of wealth, so people spend less. [[r]]They push interest rates up, which holds back borrowing and spending. [[x]]And they make domestic goods dearer abroad, so net exports fall.
beats.as: [[a]]Aggregate supply is the output firms will produce at each price level. [[sr]]In the short run, wages and other input prices are slow to change. Higher prices raise profit, so output rises: the supply curve slopes up. [[lr]]In the long run, wages catch up. Output depends only on resources and technology, so supply is vertical at potential GDP.
beats.adas: [[a]]Put them together. [[eq]]Short-run equilibrium is where aggregate demand meets short-run supply. [[lr]]When that point also sits on the long-run supply line, the economy is at potential GDP. [[p]]Here, real GDP is one hundred, and the price level is one hundred.
beats.infl: [[a]]Suppose aggregate demand rises: lower taxes, more government spending, or faster money growth. [[shift]]The curve shifts right. [[eq]]Output moves above potential, and prices rise. That is an inflationary gap. [[wage]]Tight labor markets push wages up, [[sras]]so short-run supply shifts up and left. [[end]]Output returns to potential, at a permanently higher price level.
beats.rec: [[a]]Now aggregate demand falls: weak confidence, or higher taxes. [[shift]]The curve shifts left. [[eq]]Output drops below potential, and price pressure eases. That is a recessionary gap, with high unemployment. [[wage]]Slowly, wages fall, [[sras]]and short-run supply shifts down and right, [[end]]until output returns to potential at a lower price level.
beats.stag: [[a]]A different shock hits supply. [[shift]]Say oil prices jump. Costs rise, and short-run supply shifts up and left. [[eq]]Output falls, while prices rise. That is stagflation. [[tr]]It is hard on policy makers, because the cures for unemployment and for inflation pull in opposite directions.
beats.growth: [[a]]Potential GDP grows when the economy's capacity grows. [[pf]]The production function links output to labor, capital, and technology. [[l]]More workers, or more hours. [[k]]More capital, or better capital. [[t]]And total factor productivity: producing more from the same inputs. [[sg]]Sustainable growth is growth in the labor force, plus growth in labor productivity. If the labor force grows one percent a year, and productivity two percent, sustainable growth is about three percent.
beats.wrap: [[w1]]GDP counts final output, and equals spending and income. [[w2]]Real GDP is nominal GDP divided by the deflator. [[w3]]Aggregate demand slopes down, short-run supply slopes up, and long-run supply is vertical. [[w4]]Demand shocks create gaps that wages slowly close, supply shocks cause stagflation, and growth comes from labor, capital and technology.
